etymology: Assyrian royal name (Sin-ahhe-eriba, the moon-god has replaced the brothers); king of Assyria who invaded Judah in the days of Hezekiah.
biblical_def: Sennacherib was king of Assyria who invaded Judah in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, took the fenced cities, and sent his army against Jerusalem. By his commander Rabshakeh he hurled blasphemies against the living God, boasting that no god of any nation had delivered its people from the hand of Assyria, and that the LORD of Israel would be no different. Hezekiah spread the threatening letter before the LORD in the temple and prayed; and the LORD answered through Isaiah that Sennacherib should not come into the city nor shoot an arrow there, for the King of Assyria had reproached the Holy One of Israel. That night the angel of the LORD went out and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred fourscore and five thousand; and Sennacherib departed, returned to Nineveh, and was slain by his own sons as he worshipped in the house of his god Nisroch. The whole account is a monument to the truth that the boasting of the proud comes to nothing against the God of heaven, that He defends His people for His own name’s sake, and that the arm of flesh, however vast, withers before the living God. The dictionary honors the record of Sennacherib as a standing proof that the LORD reigns, that He hears the prayer of His afflicted people, and that He brings down the high looks of the proud.
webster_summary: King of Assyria who invaded Judah under Hezekiah and blasphemed the living God; the LORD smote his host by the angel, and he was slain by his own sons.

corruption_summary: Sennacherib’s defeat is dismissed as legend or explained away by mere plague; Scripture records the LORD’s direct judgment on the blasphemer who reproached Him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the rationalist dismissal of the account—treating the destruction of the Assyrian host as legend, or explaining it away as a natural plague that the historians dressed in religious language. Scripture is plain: the angel of the LORD went out and smote a hundred fourscore and five thousand in the camp (2 Kgs 19:35; 2 Chr 32:21). The deliverance was a direct judgment of God upon a king who had reproached the living God (2 Kgs 19:16), not a coincidence of disease.

The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the proudest powers of earth and His faithfulness to defend His people for His own name’s sake. Sennacherib boasted that no god had delivered a nation from his hand, and the LORD answered that He would defend Jerusalem and that the Assyrian should not shoot an arrow there (Isa 37:33). The arm of flesh, however vast, withers before the God of heaven; the prayer of His afflicted people is heard; and the blasphemer who lifts himself against the Holy One of Israel is brought down. The record stands as a perpetual witness that the LORD reigns and that He resisteth the proud.

etymology: Assyrian royal name; the king of Assyria (also called Pul in Scripture) who carried away the tribes beyond Jordan and Galilee.
biblical_def: Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, called Pul in the Scriptures, was the powerful Assyrian monarch whom the LORD used as His rod against a faithless Israel. When Menahem king of Israel gave Pul a thousand talents of silver that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom, the tribute only delayed judgment. Later, when Pekah reigned, Tiglath-pileser came and took Ijon, and Abel-beth-maachah, and the cities of Naphtali, and carried the people captive to Assyria—the first great deportation of the northern tribes. And when Ahaz king of Judah, threatened by Syria and Israel, hired Tiglath-pileser with the treasures of the temple to deliver him, the Assyrian came, but distressed him and strengthened him not, for Ahaz had trusted the arm of Assyria rather than the LORD. The Chronicler records that God stirred up the spirit of Tiglath-pileser to carry away the transjordan tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh, because they had transgressed against the God of their fathers and gone a whoring after the gods of the peoples whom God destroyed before them. The dictionary honors the record of Tiglath-pileser as a testimony that the LORD wields even pagan empires as His instruments of chastisement upon His covenant people, and that to trust the arm of flesh against the LORD is to be distressed by the very power one hired.

corruption_summary: Tiglath-pileser is read as mere imperial conqueror in a political history; Scripture names him the LORD’s rod of chastisement upon a faithless people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the merely political-historical reading that treats Tiglath-pileser as one more ambitious conqueror in the rise of Assyrian power, subordinating the Chronicler’s theological judgment to the metrics of empire. Scripture sees deeper: the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul to carry away the transjordan tribes because they had transgressed against the God of their fathers (1 Chr 5:26). The conqueror’s ambition was the unwitting instrument of the LORD’s chastisement.

The principle to recover is the LORD’s sovereign use of pagan empires as the rod of His anger. He calls Assyria the rod of mine anger, the staff in their hand is mine indignation (Isa 10:5)—a nation that knew Him not, yet served His purpose against a faithless covenant people. The account also warns against trusting the arm of flesh: Ahaz hired Tiglath-pileser against his enemies, but the Assyrian came and distressed him and strengthened him not (2 Chr 28:20), for he had leaned on Assyria rather than the LORD. To use the world against the world, forsaking God, is to be wounded by the very power one trusted.

etymology: Name of the giant king of Bashan, of the remnant of the Rephaim, defeated by Israel under Moses.
biblical_def: Og was the giant king of Bashan, one of the last of the remnant of the Rephaim, whom Israel defeated under Moses on the east of Jordan, in the days before the crossing into Canaan. When Israel turned to go up by the way of Bashan, Og came out against them to battle at Edrei; and the LORD said unto Moses, Fear him not: for I have delivered him into thy hand, and all his people, and his land. So Israel smote him, and his sons, and all his people, until there was none left alive, and possessed his land. The Scripture marks his greatness as a sign of the victory: his bedstead was a bedstead of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits broad, a witness to his giant stature. The conquest of Og, with that of Sihon king of the Amorites, became a standing theme of Israel’s praise: the Psalms recount that the LORD smote great kings, Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og the king of Bashan, for His mercy endureth for ever. The dictionary honors the record of Og as a monument to the LORD’s power to deliver the giants of the earth into the hands of His people, that no stature of flesh, however towering, can stand against the God who goes before His own; and as a perpetual ground of praise that the LORD remembered His people in their low estate and smote the mighty for their sakes.

corruption_summary: Og is dismissed as legendary giant-lore; Scripture records a real king really defeated, a monument to the LORD’s power over the mighty of the earth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the dismissal of Og as mere legend—the giant of folklore, the iron bedstead as a tall tale. But Scripture records him soberly as a real king of a real land, the last of the remnant of giants (Deu 3:11), whom Israel really defeated at Edrei and whose territory they really possessed. The Psalms count his fall among the LORD’s historical mercies to Israel (Psa 136:20), not among myths.

The principle to recover is the power of God to deliver the mightiest of the earth into the hands of His people. The LORD bade Moses, Fear him not: for I have delivered him into thy hand (Num 21:34), and so He did, until none was left remaining (Deu 3:3). Og’s towering stature only magnified the victory: no height of flesh can stand against the God who goes before His own. The conquest of Og therefore became a perpetual ground of praise, that the LORD remembered His people in their low estate and smote great kings for their sake, for His mercy endureth for ever.

etymology: Hebrew repha’im; a race of giants dwelling in Canaan and beyond Jordan before Israel.
biblical_def: The Rephaim were a race of giants who dwelt in Canaan and the lands beyond Jordan before Israel came to possess them. Scripture names them among the peoples whom the LORD dispossessed: a people great, and many, and tall, counted giants as the Anakim. Og king of Bashan is named as the last of the remnant of the Rephaim, and the valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem bore their name. The Rephaim, with the Anakim, the Emim, and the Zamzummim, were the giant nations whose stature made the spies who searched Canaan say they were as grasshoppers in their own sight; the fear of these giants was among the chief causes of Israel’s unbelief at Kadesh, when they refused to go up and possess the land. Yet the LORD had said that He would dispossess them, and so He did, destroying them before His people as He had destroyed them before Esau and Lot in their lands. The Rephaim stand in Scripture as a figure of the great and terrible obstacles that loom before the people of God, which faith overcomes and unbelief magnifies. The dictionary honors the record of the Rephaim as a testimony that the LORD gives His people the land in the face of giants, that the obstacles which unbelief counts insurmountable are nothing before Him, and that the fear of giants is conquered not by the strength of Israel but by the promise of God.
webster_summary: A race of giants in Canaan and beyond Jordan before Israel; their stature fed Israel’s unbelief, yet the LORD dispossessed them before His people.

corruption_summary: The Rephaim are dismissed as myth or made the stuff of speculative legend; Scripture treats them soberly as real nations the LORD dispossessed before His people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite errors attend the Rephaim. The first dismisses them as myth, the giants of folklore with no place in sober history. The second runs to the other extreme, spinning speculative legend and esoteric theories around them, far beyond what Scripture says. The Bible itself is restrained: it names them as real nations, great and tall, whom the LORD dispossessed before Israel, Esau, and Lot (Deu 2:11), with Og as the last of their remnant (Deu 3:11).

The principle to recover is the victory of faith over the giants that unbelief magnifies. At Kadesh the spies saw the giants, the sons of Anak, and counted themselves as grasshoppers (Num 13:33), and their fear bred the unbelief that kept a generation out of the land. Yet the LORD had promised to dispossess these very giants, and Joshua, who feared them not, bade the people go up against the land of the giants (Jos 17:15). The Rephaim stand as a figure of every great and terrible obstacle before the people of God: faith, resting on the promise, sees them already delivered into Israel’s hand; unbelief, looking at its own strength, sees only grasshoppers before giants.

etymology: Hebrew Pelishtim; the people of the coastal plain of Canaan, perennial enemies of Israel.
biblical_def: The Philistines were the people of the southwestern coastal plain of Canaan, organized in five lordships—Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron—and the perennial enemies of Israel through the days of the Judges and the early monarchy. They oppressed Israel in the time of Samson, captured the ark of the covenant in the days of Eli, though the LORD plagued them until they sent it back, and warred against Israel under Saul, who fell before them on Mount Gilboa. Their champion Goliath of Gath defied the armies of the living God, until David, with a sling and a stone and the name of the LORD of hosts, laid him low. The Philistines worshipped Dagon, before whose image the ark of the LORD cast the idol down and broke it. They are a recurring figure in Scripture of the uncircumcised enemy who defies the people and the God of Israel, mighty in iron and in arms, yet ever brought low when the LORD arises for His people. David at last subdued them. The dictionary honors the record of the Philistines as a testimony that the enemies of God’s people, however armed and confident, fall before the LORD of hosts; that the ark of God needs no defending, for it judges the idol in its own temple; and that the battle is the LORD’s, who saveth not with sword and spear.

corruption_summary: The word Philistine is borrowed as a label for cultural ignorance, severing it from the biblical record of the LORD’s victory over His people’s enemies.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The chief drift is linguistic: the word Philistine has been borrowed into common speech as a label for a person hostile or indifferent to culture and learning, a sense entirely foreign to the Bible. This is a borrowing, not a corruption of doctrine, but it can obscure the biblical record, in which the Philistines are a real and formidable nation, mighty in arms, the perennial oppressors of Israel.

The principle to recover is that the enemies of God’s people, however armed and confident, fall before the LORD of hosts. The Philistines had iron and chariots and a champion nine feet tall, yet Goliath, who defied the armies of the living God (1 Sam 17:26), was felled by a shepherd’s sling, that all might know the battle is the LORD’s, who saveth not with sword and spear (1 Sam 17:47). And when they took the ark, their god Dagon fell broken before it (1 Sam 5:3): the ark of God needs no defending, for it judges the idol in its own temple. The record of the Philistines preaches that the LORD arises for His people and brings the proud enemy low.

etymology: Hebrew Uzzah, strength; the man smitten for touching the ark of God.
biblical_def: Uzzah was the son of Abinadab who was smitten dead by the LORD for putting forth his hand to the ark of God when the oxen stumbled. David and all Israel were bringing up the ark from the house of Abinadab on a new cart, with music and rejoicing; but when they came to the threshingfloor of Nachon, the oxen shook the ark, and Uzzah put forth his hand to take hold of it. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God smote him there for his error, and he died by the ark of God. David was displeased and afraid, and asked, How shall the ark of the LORD come to me? He left it in the house of Obededom for three months, where it brought blessing, and then brought it up rightly, carried by the Levites upon their shoulders as the law had commanded, with sacrifice and great joy. The death of Uzzah is a solemn lesson: the ark was to be borne by the Levites, not carted as the Philistines had carted it, and not touched by any common hand; the LORD’s holiness is not to be served by man’s good intentions in man’s own way. The dictionary honors the record of Uzzah as a fearful witness to the holiness of God and the necessity of worshipping Him as He has commanded, not as we think best—the very root of the regulative principle, that good intentions do not sanctify forbidden means.
webster_summary: The man smitten dead for steadying the ark with his hand; a solemn witness that God’s holiness must be served His own way, not by man’s good intentions.

corruption_summary: Uzzah’s death is judged unfair, faulting God for harshness; Scripture shows the holiness of God and the sin of serving Him by forbidden means, however well-meant.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the instinct that judges God unjust in Uzzah’s death—that the man meant only to help, that his intentions were good, that the LORD was harsh. But this complaint arraigns the Judge of all the earth at the bar of fallen sentiment. The Law had plainly commanded that the ark be borne on the shoulders of the Levites and that no common hand touch the holy thing, lest he die (Num 4:15). The whole enterprise was already in disobedience, carting the ark as the Philistines had done.

The principle to recover is the holiness of God and the regulative principle of worship—that God is to be served as He has commanded, not as man thinks best. David himself came to see it: the LORD made a breach upon them because they sought Him not after the due order (1 Chr 15:13), and the second time the Levites bore the ark rightly, with sacrifice and joy. Good intentions do not sanctify forbidden means; the worship of a holy God is governed by His word, not by our sincerity. Uzzah’s death stands as a fearful and merciful warning that the LORD will be sanctified in them that come nigh Him.

etymology: From conquest + Canaan; the taking of the promised land by Israel under Joshua.
biblical_def: The conquest of Canaan is the taking of the promised land by Israel under Joshua, after the forty years in the wilderness, in fulfilment of the oath the LORD sware to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Israel crossed Jordan on dry ground as the priests bare the ark, took Jericho when its walls fell at the trumpet and the shout, and, after the sin of Achan was purged, went on to subdue the kings of the south and the north, until Joshua took the whole land according to all that the LORD said unto Moses. The conquest was the LORD’s war and the LORD’s gift: He fought for Israel, drove out the nations before them, and gave them a land for which they did not labour, cities they built not, and vineyards they planted not. It was also an act of righteous judgment upon the Canaanite nations, whose iniquity was now full—a people given over to idolatry, child sacrifice, and abominations, whom the LORD cast out before His people, that Israel might not learn their ways. The dictionary honors the conquest of Canaan as the fulfilment of covenant promise, the gift of rest to the people of God, and the righteous judgment of the LORD upon a ripened wickedness—a foreshadowing of the rest that remaineth for the people of God and of the final judgment by which the Lord shall give His saints their inheritance and cast out the wicked for ever.

corruption_summary: The conquest is condemned as genocide by modern moral judgment, or spiritualized away; Scripture presents it as covenant fulfilment and righteous judgment on ripened sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the moral objection. The chief corruption is the modern charge that the conquest was genocide, an atrocity to be condemned by the conscience of a later age. This judgment sets fallen man as judge over God and forgets two truths Scripture presses. First, the LORD is the Judge of all the earth, and the conquest was His righteous judgment upon nations whose iniquity was full (Gen 15:16)—a people given to idolatry, child sacrifice, and abomination, cast out for their own wickedness, not for Israel’s righteousness (Deu 9:5).

Second, the conquest was the fulfilment of covenant promise and the gift of rest. The LORD gave Israel a land for which they did not labour, cities they built not (Jos 24:13), and not one good thing failed of all He had spoken (Jos 21:45). To spiritualize the conquest away, on the other hand, empties it of its historical reality and its place in redemption. The dictionary holds both: the conquest was real history, righteous judgment on ripened sin, and covenant gift—a foreshadowing of the rest that remaineth for the people of God and of the last judgment, when the Lord shall give His saints their inheritance and cast out the wicked for ever.

etymology: From trans- (across) + Jordan; the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh who settled east of Jordan.
biblical_def: The transjordan tribes were Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, who received their inheritance east of the river Jordan, in the lands of Sihon and Og which Israel had conquered. Having much cattle, they saw that the land of Jazer and Gilead was good for cattle, and asked Moses to give them that land for a possession and not bring them over Jordan. Moses, fearing they would discourage their brethren as the spies had done, charged them; but they pledged to send their armed men over Jordan to fight alongside their brethren until the land was subdued, and to return only when Israel had inherited. They kept their word: their warriors crossed over and fought through the conquest before returning to their families and possessions east of Jordan. Later, when they built a great altar by Jordan, the other tribes nearly went to war, fearing apostasy, until it was explained as a witness of their unity in the worship of the LORD, not a rival altar. In the end the transjordan tribes, exposed on the frontier, were among the first carried away by Assyria for their idolatry. The dictionary honors the record of the transjordan tribes as a study in the danger of choosing one’s inheritance by the eye and the cattle rather than by the promise, and as a witness that the people of God, however divided by rivers and borders, are one in the worship of the LORD and bound to bear one another’s burdens in the common warfare.
webster_summary: Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh, who settled east of Jordan; they fought for their brethren in the conquest, yet, exposed on the frontier, were first into Assyrian exile.

corruption_summary: The transjordan settlement is read as a mere land deal; Scripture weighs it as a choice by sight over promise and a study in the unity and warning of God’s people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the flattening of the account into a mere real-estate transaction—tribes choosing good grazing land for their herds, with no spiritual weight. But Scripture frames the choice as a spiritual question. Reuben and Gad chose by the eye and the cattle (Num 32:1), settling short of the promised inheritance across Jordan, and Moses warned that to shrink from the common warfare would be sin against the LORD, and be sure your sin will find you out (Num 32:23).

The principle to recover is twofold. First, the danger of choosing one’s portion by sight rather than by promise: the transjordan tribes, exposed on the frontier, were among the first carried into exile, having transgressed and gone a whoring after the gods of the land (1 Chr 5:25). Second, the unity of God’s people across every border. Their warriors crossed Jordan to fight for their brethren, and their altar by the river was raised not as a rival sanctuary but as a witness that the LORD is God (Jos 22:34), binding the tribes in one worship though divided by the river. The people of God, however scattered, are one, and are to bear one another’s burdens in the common warfare.

etymology: From accursed; the Hebrew cherem, a thing devoted to destruction and forbidden to Israel, as in the sin of Achan (Jos 7).
biblical_def: The accursed thing is the rendering of the Hebrew cherem, a thing devoted to destruction and under the ban—set apart by the LORD for ruin, and forbidden to be taken or kept. At the fall of Jericho the LORD commanded that the city and all its spoil be wholly devoted: the silver and gold to the treasury of the LORD, and all else destroyed, and that Israel keep themselves from the accursed thing lest they make the camp of Israel a curse and trouble it. But Achan took of the accursed thing—a goodly Babylonish garment, silver, and a wedge of gold—and hid them in his tent; and the anger of the LORD was kindled against all Israel, so that they were smitten before the men of Ai. Israel could not stand before their enemies until the sin was found out and purged. The accursed thing teaches that the sin of one may bring guilt and chastisement upon the whole people, that what God has devoted to destruction is deadly to covet and keep, and that hidden sin must be brought to light and put away before the people of God can prosper. It is a type of the sin that troubles the camp, the secret covetousness that defiles the whole. The dictionary honors this record as a solemn lesson in corporate holiness, the danger of covetousness, and the necessity of putting away sin from the midst of God’s people, that the LORD may be with them in the day of battle.

corruption_summary: The account is judged unfair for punishing the many for one man’s sin; Scripture teaches corporate holiness and the deadly defilement of hidden, covetous sin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the modern objection that it was unjust for Israel to suffer, and Achan’s household to perish, for one man’s sin—the protest of an individualism that denies any corporate solidarity in guilt or grace. But Scripture everywhere knows the solidarity of a people: in Adam all sinned, in Achan all Israel was troubled. The sin of one devoted thing taken made the whole camp accursed, so that Israel could not stand before their enemies (Jos 7:13).

The principle to recover is corporate holiness and the deadly nature of hidden sin. The LORD had warned Israel to keep from the accursed thing, lest they make the camp of Israel a curse and trouble it (Jos 6:18); Achan’s secret covetousness defiled the whole. The lesson is not that God is unjust but that sin among the people of God is a serious and infectious thing, that hidden sin must be brought to light and put away, and that the camp cannot prosper while it harbours what God has cursed. It is a type of the covetousness and concealed sin that still troubles the church, and a summons to put away the accursed thing, that the LORD may be with His people.

etymology: From mighty + men; the valiant warriors of David, and the term for men of valour in Scripture.
biblical_def: The mighty men were the valiant warriors gathered about David, his band of heroes whose exploits are recorded in the books of Samuel and Chronicles. They came to him first in the cave of Adullam, when every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented gathered to him, and he became a captain over them; and out of that desperate company the LORD made an army of mighty men. The chief of them—Adino, Eleazar, Shammah, and the rest—did valiant deeds: one slew eight hundred at one time, another held a plot of ground against the Philistines when the people fled, another smote a lion in a pit on a snowy day. Three of them broke through the host of the Philistines to draw water from the well of Bethlehem at David’s longing, but David would not drink it, pouring it out unto the LORD, for it was the blood of men who had jeoparded their lives. The mighty men are a picture of what grace makes of the broken and the desperate: gathered to the LORD’s anointed in their distress, they are transformed into valiant warriors, bound to their captain in loyal love, and made the instruments of his victories. The dictionary honors the mighty men of David as a type of the soldiers of Christ, the true Son of David, who gathers the distressed and the indebted to Himself and makes of them, by grace, mighty men of valour in His warfare.

corruption_summary: The mighty men are reduced to mere military legend; Scripture sets them as a picture of grace transforming the broken into valiant servants of the LORD’s anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the reduction of the mighty men to mere military legend—a heroic muster-roll of ancient warriors with no spiritual significance. But Scripture frames them as a work of grace. They came to David not as polished soldiers but as the distressed, the indebted, the discontented (1 Sam 22:2), a desperate company gathered to the LORD’s rejected anointed in the cave; and out of that company the LORD made an army of valiant men.

The principle to recover is what grace makes of the broken who gather to the LORD’s anointed. The mighty men were bound to David in loyal love—Thine are we, David, and on thy side, for thy God helpeth thee (1 Chr 12:18)—and their valour flowed from that allegiance. They jeoparded their lives for him; he poured out their costly gift unto the LORD (2 Sam 23:16). So they are a type of the soldiers of Christ, the true Son of David, who gathers the distressed and indebted to Himself in their need and makes of them, by His grace, mighty men of valour in His warfare. The desperate who come to Him are not left as they were; grace transforms them into faithful servants.
